B1 Scoping doc — Instrument activation metric + dashboard
Title
- Define & instrument the single most meaningful activation event and ship an always-on activation dashboard.

Background / why now
- We lack a clear, reliable activation KPI and funnel visualization. That prevents us from measuring improvements to onboarding and early product value, slows decision-making, and makes prioritization fuzzy. Instrumenting a single activation event and dashboard gives immediate alignment and enables fast experiments.

Objective
- Agree on one activation definition, reliably collect the event with required properties, establish a baseline, and deliver a dashboard that shows activation rate and funnel conversion by cohort/source.

Primary success metrics (what “done” looks like)
- Activation event definition agreed and documented.
- Activation event instrumented in prod with >=95% tracking coverage for new users.
- Dashboard live showing: activation rate (new users → activated) daily, 7/30-day cohort view, and funnel stages with conversion rates.
- Baseline activation rate calculated and shared with stakeholders.
- Alert/monitoring for instrumentation regressions (missing events, sudden drop) configured.

Secondary metrics (nice-to-have)
- Activation by channel/campaign, device, onboarding variant.
- Time-to-activation distribution and median TTFV.

Scope (in/out)
- In scope: Define activation event, implement instrumentation (client/server as needed), QA/validate events, build dashboard, compute baseline, communicate results.
- Out of scope: Large product changes to drive activation (these follow from insights) and long-term retention experiments (separate workstream).

Owners & stakeholders
- Product owner: [Your name] (overall)
- Engineering lead: [eng lead name]
- Data/Analytics: [data lead name]
- Design: [design lead name] (for any UI tags / experiment flags)
- CS / Growth: [names] (for campaign mapping)
- QA: [qa lead]
- Exec update: [manager name]

Data & instrumentation spec (example)
- Event name: user_activated
- Who fires it: client (web/mobile) or backend when user completes meaningful action
- Required properties:
  - user_id (string)
  - anonymous_id / session_id (if applicable)
  - timestamp
  - activation_path (string) — e.g., "guided_task", "manual", "import"
  - onboarding_step (string) — last step before activation
  - campaign_source (string) — UTM or internal source
  - device_type / platform
  - experiment_flag (string/boolean) — optional
- Event semantics: event must be triggered once per user (or mark first_time=true) when user completes the activation action that correlates with retention.

Funnel definition (suggested)
- F0: New account created (or first relevant session)
- F1: Completed onboarding step X (if applicable)
- F2: user_activated (primary activation event)
- F3: First paid or second-week retention (later usage)
- Dashboard should show conversion % between stages and time-to-activation.

Implementation plan & tasks (7–14 day target)
Day 0–2: Discovery & alignment (1–2 days)
- Confirm proposed activation definition with Data, Eng, Growth, CS. (1 meeting)
- Pull existing event coverage and any instrumentation gaps for new users.

Day 3–6: Instrumentation & schema (2–4 days)
- Engineering: add/emit user_activated event per spec (client or backend). Add any missing properties.
- Data: add event to tracking plan; add to warehouse ingestion mapping; create a canonical event table or view.
- QA: generate test users and validate events in analytics pipeline.

Day 7–9: Dashboard & baseline (2–3 days)
- Data/Analytics: build dashboard with:
  - Activation rate (daily/rolling),
  - Funnel conversion table,
  - Cohort retention tied to activation,
  - Breakdown by source/device/experiment.
- Compute baseline for last 30/60 days and write short context note.

Day 10–14: Validate, alerting, communicate (1–3 days)
- Validate event coverage in production; fix gaps.
- Configure instrumentation alerts or monitoring (e.g., error if event count drops >30% day-over-day).
- Share dashboard + 1-page baseline with stakeholders and schedule a 15–30 min review.

Acceptance criteria (QA)
- Event appears in analytics with correct schema for test and real users.
- >95% of new users in the last X days show either activation event or explicit non-activation flag (i.e., instrumented coverage).
- Dashboard calculations match raw event counts and show baseline numbers.
- Stakeholders have signed off on the activation definition.

Risks & mitigations
- Misdefined activation: run a quick validation session with Data/CS/Growth to ensure event correlates with retention. Mitigation: require historical correlation check before finalizing.
- Instrumentation gaps: mitigate by using both client and server instrumentation where possible, adding retry logic and logging.
- Analytics latency: ensure pipeline supports near-real-time (or note delay) and set expectations for reporting cadence.

Dependencies
- Access to analytics tooling (Segment/Amplitude/Mixpanel/GA/warehouse). Please grant [data lead] and me access.
- Engineering bandwidth and a small slot in a sprint or hotfix window.
- Test/QA environment for event validation and test users.

Estimated effort
- Product: 6–10 hours (definition, QA, comms)
- Eng: 1–3 dev days (depends on current tracking)
- Data: 1–2 analyst days (dashboard + baseline)
- QA: 0.5–1 day

Communications & rollout
- Day 0: Alignment meeting + confirm timeline.
- Day 7–9: Share staging dashboard link and draft baseline.
- Day 10–14: Publish dashboard to execs/team, schedule 15–30 min review, add to weekly product update.

Deliverables
- Documented activation event definition (in tracking plan).
- Instrumented event in prod.
- Activation dashboard and baseline report.
- Short email to stakeholders summarizing baseline and proposed next experiments.

Next steps I need from you
- Confirm owners (eng/data names) or I can draft the invite to pull them in.
- Tell me which analytics tool and whether you have a team tracker/tribe + access.
- Share any existing hypotheses about what activation should be (if you already suspect a specific action).
- Approve target timeline (I recommend 10 business days by default).

I’ll draft the scoping doc for A1 (fix onboarding drop-off) next — do you want that to include proposed microcopy/UX changes and an engineering estimate, or keep it focused on problem → solution → metrics so you can assign engineering to scope?

A. Scoping doc — A1: Fix top onboarding drop-off
Title
- Reduce drop-off at onboarding step X by simplifying the UI and validation, adding contextual help, and reducing required fields.

Background / why now
- Analytics show a large drop (e.g., 40–60%) at onboarding step X. This creates a bottleneck for activation and inflates CS tickets. Small UX and validation fixes should produce a measurable lift quickly.

Objective
- Reduce drop-off at step X by 20%+ and improve time-to-activation and first-week retention.

Primary success metrics (what “done” looks like)
- Drop-off rate at step X reduced by ≥20%.
- Activation rate uplift (measured via the activation event you’re instrumenting) improves by target % (define baseline after B1).
- Support tickets related to onboarding topic reduced by 30%.

Scope (in / out)
- In scope: Simplify form fields, inline validation, microcopy/tooltips, minor layout adjustments, client-side improvements (plus any small backend changes required for validation/autofill).
- Out of scope: Full redesign of onboarding, social sign-on, large backend workflows, multi-variant experiments (can follow).

Owners & stakeholders
- Product: [Your name] (PM)
- Eng lead: [eng lead name]
- Design/UX: [design lead name]
- Data/Analytics: [data lead name] (for measurement)
- QA: [qa lead name]
- CS/Growth: [names] (feedback & success validation)

Diagnosis summary (quick)
- Where: Onboarding step X (form / screen).
- Observed behavior: High time on step, repeated field corrections, support tickets citing confusion/validation errors.
- Likely root causes: Overly many fields, unexpected validation, poor error messaging, slow client-side performance on that step.

Proposed changes (UX + microcopy)
1) Simplify fields
- Remove nonessential fields from the first-pass flow; move to progressive profiling later.
- Combine related fields (e.g., “Company name” + “Company size” -> progressive ask later).

2) Inline validation & optimistic UI
- Validate on blur with clear, inline messages.
- Show loading/processing state immediately for any server checks.

3) Contextual help / microcopy
- Add two short helper lines and one tooltip:
  - Header microcopy (below title): “This only takes 2 minutes — we’ll ask anything else later.”
  - Field-level helper example for a tricky field (placeholder & tooltip):
    - Field label: “Business ID (optional)”
    - Placeholder: “e.g., 123-456 (you can skip this for now)”
    - Tooltip text: “We use this to prefill company settings — not required to continue.”
  - Error messaging example:
    - Current generic: “Invalid input”
    - New clear message: “Looks like the phone number is missing the country code. Try +1 555 5555 or skip for now.”

4) Autofill / defaults
- If possible, prefill common values (country, language) from locale or earlier steps.

5) CTA clarity & friction reduction
- Make primary CTA clear and persistent (“Get started” vs “Next”).
- If the step is long, break it into two sub-steps or show progress “Step 2 of 4”.

6) Quick accessibility & performance checks
- Ensure keyboard focus, proper labels, and <200ms feedback on validation.

Microcopy examples (drop-in)
- Onboarding header: “Welcome — we’ll get you set up in two quick steps.”
- First helper: “Tip: you can skip optional fields and finish setup later.”
- Error on validation: “Please enter a valid email (example@company.com) or continue without one.”
- CTA: “Continue — create account”

Engineering estimate (rough)
- Frontend changes (form simplification, inline validation, microcopy, tooltips, CTA): 3–6 dev days
  - If client-side only and straightforward, closer to 3 days.
  - If needs UI kit adjustments or animations, closer to 5–6 days.
- Backend changes (server-side validation tweak, common-value autofill APIs, small support endpoints): 0.5–2 dev days
  - If current APIs already support checks, likely ~0.5–1 day.
- Data/Tracking updates (ensure onboarding steps instrumented): 0.5–1 analyst day
- QA & regression testing: 1 day
- Design/UX tasks (mockups, microcopy, review): 1–2 designer days
- Total rough effort: ~6–11 person-days across disciplines (parallelizable). Plan for a single 1–2 sprint cycle (target: 10 business days).

Implementation plan & timeline (target ~10 business days)
Day 0–2: Align & design
- 30–45 min kickoff with Eng/Design/Data/QA. Confirm scope, critical fields, and measurement plan.
- Design produces 1–2 mock variants and microcopy.

Day 3–7: Build
- Frontend implements simplified UI, inline validation, microcopy.
- Backend implements any small validation endpoints / autofill support.
- Data adds or validates instrumentation for the onboarding steps.

Day 8–9: QA & staging
- QA runs regression tests, edge cases; collect CS feedback on messages.
- Adjustments from QA & CS.

Day 10: Release & monitor
- Deploy to production (or feature flag).
- Monitor drop-off and activation metrics daily; be ready to rollback or adjust microcopy.

Acceptance criteria (QA)
- Drop-off instrumented and visible in analytics for A1 funnel stages.
- No regressions in other onboarding traffic (smoke tests pass).
- Inline errors are clear and actionable.
- >95% coverage for instrumentation of onboarding step events.
- Stakeholders sign off on launch.

Risks & mitigations
- Unexpected backend dependency: mitigate by scoping only client validations first and making backend changes minimal.
- Change exacerbates drop-off: run a small % rollout or feature flag to measure impact before full rollout.
- Miscommunication of optional vs required fields: use clear helper text and mark optional fields.

Dependencies
- Design capacity for mockups + microcopy.
- Eng bandwidth for prioritized slot in sprint.
- Data access to verify funnel and calculate drop-off reduction.
- Link to activation instrumentation (B1) so activation lift can be measured.

Deliverables
- Updated onboarding screen(s) in prod behind flag or full release.
- Updated onboarding funnel events instrumented and visible in Amplitude.
- Short post-release note with before/after metrics at Day 3 and Day 7.

B. Kickoff invite templates (send to Eng lead, Data lead, QA)
Use these to pull folks into the B1 activation work and the A1 onboarding fix. Swap names/dates/times.

30/60/90 plan — Senior Product Manager, Mobile Squad

Goal framing
- Short-term: learn context, build trust, and deliver fast credibility with one or two quick wins.
- Mid-term: align stakeholders, stabilize delivery cadence, and launch improvements that move core mobile KPIs.
- Long-term (90 days+): own roadmap, set measurable objectives, and position the squad to hit quarterly OKRs.

Days 0–30 (Learn & stabilize)
- Objectives
  - Build relationships with squad, engineering leads, design, QA, analytics, and key stakeholders (marketing, support).
  - Understand current roadmap, backlog, tech constraints, and top user pain points.
  - Identify immediate risks and quick wins.
- Actions
  - 1:1s with each direct report + key cross-functional partners (30–60 min). Ask current priorities, blockers, expectations.
  - Review analytics: DAU/MAU, retention, onboarding conversion, crashes, feature usage, funnel drop-offs.
  - Audit roadmap, active sprints, release schedule, and outstanding tech debt.
  - Run or review recent user research and top support tickets.
  - Pick 1 quick win (e.g., critical crash fix, onboarding flow tweak, or a copy change that improves conversion) and scope it.
- Metrics/Deliverables
  - Stakeholder map + decision rights document (who owns what).
  - 1–2 prioritized risks and an action plan for the quick win.
  - Draft 30–60–90 objectives shared with manager for alignment.

Days 31–60 (Align & deliver)
- Objectives
  - Deliver quick win(s), set roadmap priorities, and begin establishing processes (backlog hygiene, planning).
- Actions
  - Run a joint roadmap alignment session with PM/engineering/design and product leadership to set top priorities for next quarter.
  - Implement/track quick win and report impact.
  - Introduce or refine sprint planning, grooming cadence, and definition of done.
  - Initiate 3–5 user interviews or a small usability test to validate assumptions for a high-priority feature.
  - Define success metrics and instrumentation needs for priority features; work with analytics to fill gaps.
- Metrics/Deliverables
  - Release/impact report for the quick win (before/after metrics).
  - Prioritized roadmap draft with clear OKRs and expected outcomes.
  - Updated backlog with estimated effort and prioritized top 3 initiatives.

Days 61–90 (Own & scale)
- Objectives
  - Own and communicate the roadmap; show measurable progress toward core KPIs; set up regular stakeholder communication.
- Actions
  - Launch at least one roadmap initiative or major iteration; monitor early results and iterate.
  - Establish recurring stakeholder cadence (weekly engineering sync, biweekly roadmap review, monthly leadership update).
  - Identify areas to delegate and hire/mentor needs if squad capacity is limiting.
  - Create a 90-day retrospective and a plan for next quarter’s OKRs.
- Metrics/Deliverables
  - Demonstrable improvements toward chosen KPIs (e.g., +X% onboarding conversion, -Y% crash rate, +Z retention at 7 days).
  - Published roadmap and communication plan for the next quarter.
  - Team health check (velocity, morale, blockers) and plan to address top issues.

Suggested quick wins (pick 1–2)
- Triage and fix the top 1–3 crash reports causing highest user impact.
- Improve onboarding flow to reduce time-to-first-value — A/B test a simplified flow.
- Small UX tweak on home screen or CTA that targets conversion funnel.
- Clean up backlog: close or re-prioritize stale tickets and define acceptance criteria.

Key metrics to track (examples)
- Activation/onboarding completion rate
- 7- and 30-day retention
- DAU/MAU and session length
- Conversion (free->paid or key action)
- Crash rate and crash-free users %
- Feature adoption for launched features
- Cycle time and sprint predictability

Deliverables / metrics

- Team health report and capacity/hiring recommendations.

Suggested quick wins (pick 1–2)

- Week 4: Implement 1 quick win and present findings/next steps to manager.

- Week 7: Present proposed roadmap for next 3–6 months to manager/stakeholders.

Meetings & cadence
- Begin regular cross-functional check-ins for major initiatives.
- Establish a single source of truth for project status (shared doc/board).
- Continue weekly manager 1:1 and team syncs.

Deliverables
- Updated 90-day roadmap with milestones and owners.
- At least one implemented process change (e.g., sprint review, reporting cadence).
- Early metric improvements or documented baseline + target (e.g., speed of delivery, customer NPS, revenue-related KPI).

90 days — Deliver & Scale (Drive measurable impact)
Primary goals
- Show measurable progress against success metrics agreed with manager.
- Shift from discovery to execution/scale and strategic planning.
- Institutionalize processes and begin long-term strategy execution.

Weekly milestones
- Week 9–10: Measure results from launched initiatives; course-correct where needed.
- Week 11: Present 90-day review to manager and stakeholders: what worked, lessons, next priorities.
- Week 12: Finalize 6–12 month strategy and resource requests.

Meetings & cadence
- Quarterly planning kickoff for longer-term roadmap.
- Regular reporting on KPIs tied to business outcomes.

Deliverables
- 90-day review document: achievements, metrics, risks, and next steps.
- 6–12 month strategic roadmap with resource asks and success criteria.
- Delegation/people plan so you can focus on strategy.

Suggested success metrics (pick what fits your role)
- Delivery: % of projects on-time, cycle time improvements.
- Impact: revenue uplift, cost savings, customer satisfaction (NPS/CSAT).
- Team: employee engagement/retention, time-to-hire for open roles.
- Operational: process adoption rate, mean time to resolve critical issues.

- Tackle a small technical debt or customer complaint that’s quick to resolve.

1:1 agenda template (30 min)
- 5 min: Personal check-in.
- 10 min: Status updates + blockers.
- 10 min: Career/feedback discussion or coaching.
- 5 min: Next steps and commitments.

Risks & mitigations
- Risk: Overcommitting too many initiatives. Mitigation: Prioritize ruthlessly; use 1–2 success metrics.
- Risk: Not building stakeholder buy-in. Mitigation: frequent short updates and early wins.
- Risk: Micromanaging. Mitigation: set clear outcomes, delegate authority and follow up on metrics.

0–30 days — Learn, align, and quick wins

- Documented release readiness checklist and RACI for launches.

Primary goals
- Launch Feature A and put Feature B on a clear path to launch (aim for both this quarter if realistic).
- Demonstrate measurable improvement in delivery velocity metrics.
- Present a 90-day review with achievements, KPIs, and a 6–12 month product roadmap.

- Week 12:

- Roadmap for next 6–12 months and a people/resource plan.

Suggested success metrics to track (examples)
- Sprint completion rate (% of committed stories completed).
- Average cycle time / lead time.

- Feature-specific metrics: activation, retention, conversion, or revenue impact.
- Release frequency (# releases per month).
- Team health: engagement/feedback, unplanned work %.

RACI (high level)
- Product (you): vision, prioritization, PRD, acceptance criteria, launch owner.

30 days — Listen, learn, and stabilize
- Primary objective: Build trust and situational awareness; understand team capabilities, product status, stakeholders, and current priorities.
- Key actions:
  - Schedule one-on-ones with each direct report (60 min) and document: role, strengths, current work, blockers, career goals, preferred feedback style.
  - Hold a team kickoff (30–60 min) to introduce yourself, share your working style, set immediate expectations, and invite feedback (see sample script below).
  - Map stakeholders (engineering leads, design, sales, marketing, CS, execs). For each, capture: interest, influence, current relationship, communication preference.
  - Audit current roadmap, backlog, metrics, OKRs, recent releases, and any outstanding commitments. Read docs, product analytics, support tickets, and recent post-mortems.
  - Join recurring cross‑functional ceremonies (planning, standups, stakeholder syncs) to observe dynamics.
  - Identify 2–3 “quick wins” that unblock the team or demonstrate immediate value (e.g., clarify a roadmap item, remove a recurring meeting, fix a high-impact bug).
- Success metrics:
  - All 1:1s complete and notes captured.
  - Stakeholder map completed.
  - Top 3 short-term priorities identified and communicated.
  - At least one quick win delivered.
- Risks & mitigations:
  - Risk: Moving too fast and losing buy-in. Mitigate by asking questions, validating assumptions, and prioritizing listening.
  - Risk: Over-scheduling. Protect blocks for deep work—set repeating strategic time.

60 days — Align, set direction, and start executing
- Primary objective: Define/communicate a clear product direction and initial roadmap; improve team processes; start delivering improvements.
- Key actions:
  - Synthesize learnings into a 30–60 day readout for stakeholders: current state, key opportunities, proposed priorities, and trade-offs.
  - Run a cross‑functional alignment session (workshop) to agree on top customer problems, success metrics, and a draft roadmap for the next 3–6 months.
  - Introduce (or refine) a prioritization framework (RICE, Opportunity Scoring, or weighted scoring) and apply it to backlog.
  - Set clear goals/KPIs for team (top 3 measurable outcomes) and link to company OKRs.
  - Start delegating ownership of specific initiatives and define success criteria for each.
  - Establish or standardize team rituals: weekly product sync, roadmap review, sprint planning, and monthly review with stakeholders.
  - Begin running small experiments and iterating on feature launches.
- Success metrics:
  - Shared roadmap and prioritization visible to stakeholders.
  - Team has clear owners and success metrics for each initiative.
  - At least one larger deliverable or experiment in progress with metrics baseline.
- Risks & mitigations:
  - Risk: Stakeholder misalignment. Mitigate with documented decisions, clear trade-offs, and a RACI for major initiatives.
  - Risk: Team burnout from too many simultaneous priorities. Mitigate by limiting WIP and ensuring clear capacity planning.

90 days — Deliver, measure, and scale
- Primary objective: Demonstrate measurable impact; institutionalize processes; create a 6–12 month product plan.
- Key actions:
  - Measure outcomes from initial experiments/releases and iterate based on data.
  - Publish a 6–12 month product plan/roadmap with milestones and dependencies; present to execs and stakeholders.
  - Formalize team development: career plans, delegation structure, and a feedback cadence (quarterly reviews, promotion criteria).
  - Put stakeholder governance in place: monthly steering, decision log, and escalation paths.
  - Optimize cross-functional execution: refine handoffs, reduce blockers, and improve release predictability.
  - Identify hiring or upskilling needs and begin recruiting or training plans if needed.
- Success metrics:
  - Evidence of impact on 2–3 key metrics (e.g., retention, conversion, NPS, time-to-market).
  - Stakeholders aligned on roadmap and decision log established.
  - Clear career development plans for team members.
- Risks & mitigations:
  - Risk: Metrics not moving. Mitigate by re-evaluating hypotheses, increasing experiment velocity, and reallocating resources.
  - Risk: Confusion on priorities. Mitigate by re-communicating OKRs and visible prioritization.

Practical items you can use now
- Suggested meeting cadence

  - Weekly team sync — 30–45 min (status, blockers, wins).

Tips for leading former peers & handling imposter feelings
- Be explicit about role changes: acknowledge you were a peer and say what will change (e.g., “I’m here to support your growth and remove roadblocks”).
- Maintain humility and curiosity: ask for input and credit people publicly.
- Delegate authority with clarity: assign owners and success criteria rather than micromanaging.

30/60/90-day plan (objectives, key actions, success measures)

Days 0–30 — Listen, learn, stabilize
- Primary objective: build trust, gather facts, and identify 1–2 quick wins.
- Key actions:
  - 1:1s with each direct report (60–90 min first meeting): role, current work, blockers, career goals, what they need from you.
  - 1:1s with key stakeholders: Eng manager(s), Design, Sales, CS, Marketing, Finance, and your manager — focus on expectations and success metrics.

  - Run product demos / sit with support to hear real customer issues.
  - Map stakeholders and current dependencies.
  - Identify candidate quick wins (bug fixes, small UX improvements, unblock blocked release).
- Deliverables / artifacts:
  - 30-day readout: top 3 opportunities, top 3 risks, recommended 30/60/90 priorities.
  - Schedule recurring cadences: team standup, leadership sync, product review.
- Success measures (how you know this phase worked):
  - All 1:1s completed and notes captured.
  - Clear list of prioritized quick wins and plan to deliver 1–2 in next 30 days.
  - Baseline metrics established (DAU/MAU, retention, NPS, velocity, cycle time).
  - Team feels heard (pulse check).

Days 31–60 — Set direction and align
- Primary objective: define priorities, start delivering quick wins, and align the team and stakeholders around a focused roadmap.
- Key actions:
  - Finalize and socialize a prioritized 90-day roadmap and top-level OKRs.
  - Present proposed priorities to leadership and incorporate feedback.
  - Implement 1–2 process improvements (e.g., definition of ready/done, decision framework, release checklist).
  - Start regular product reviews (show metrics and experiments/feature performance).
  - Continue 1:1s and begin development-focused coaching for PMs.
  - Launch targeted customer interviews or usage-analysis for key hypotheses.
- Deliverables / artifacts:
  - Prioritized roadmap and OKRs (with owners and success metrics).
  - A/B test or experiment plan for a top hypothesis.
  - Team RACI for critical initiatives.
- Success measures:
  - Stakeholder sign-off on priorities.
  - Delivery of identified quick wins and measurable uptick in a chosen metric (usage, conversion, bug count reduction).
  - Clear improvements in cycle time, release stability, or team throughput.

Days 61–90 — Execute, measure impact, and scale
- Primary objective: deliver measurable outcomes, institutionalize improvements, and prepare the next quarter’s strategy.
- Key actions:
  - Execute on roadmap items and track OKRs weekly.
  - Review outcomes from experiments and iterate.
  - Formalize career / development plans for direct reports; hire if necessary.
  - Standardize reporting to leadership (dashboard + concise summary).
  - Run a 90-day review with leadership and the team: outcomes, learnings, next priorities.
- Deliverables / artifacts:
  - 90-day outcomes report (what shipped, impact vs. targets, lessons learned).
  - Roadmap for next quarter + resourcing plan.
  - Hiring / org recommendations if gaps remain.
- Success measures:

  - Measurable business impact from shipped work (e.g., X% lift in conversion, Y% reduction in churn).
  - Team cadence and processes adopted and sustainable.

First-team meeting script (60 minutes — first all-hands / kickoff)

Timing and overall flow: 60 minutes total. Optionally extend to 75 if you want deeper conversation.

Agenda
- 0–5 min: Welcome & context
- 5–20 min: Individual quick intros (team)
- 20–35 min: Your vision, immediate priorities, and expectations
- 35–55 min: Listening session — guided discussion and capturable feedback
- 55–60 min: Next steps, actions, and close

Script (copy-paste and personalize)
- Opening (0–5 min)
  - “Thanks everyone — I’m really excited to be here. I want this to be a collaborative team where we deliver great outcomes and people grow. Today I want to introduce myself, learn about you, and share the initial priorities I’ll be focusing on. My door is open — I’ll be scheduling 1:1s with each of you so we can go deeper.”

- Team intros (5–20 min) — ~2 minutes per person
  - Ask each person to answer briefly: name/role, what they’re currently focused on, one thing working well, one pain point, and one thing they’d like to learn/do this year.
  - Prompt: “Take 60–90 seconds each — please share the thing you most want me to know about your work or where you need help.”

- Your priorities & expectations (20–35 min)
  - “Top priorities for the first 90 days: 1) listen & align on priorities; 2) deliver 1–2 quick wins that unblock the team or customers; 3) create a clear, measurable roadmap and success metrics. I’ll be focused on clearing blockers, helping prioritize, improving our delivery process, and coaching PMs to make bigger product decisions.”
  - Share communication rhythm: “Weekly product sync, monthly roadmap review, 1:1s weekly/biweekly. I prefer asynchronous updates for status unless something needs a decision.”
  - Expectations: ownership model (who decides what), definition of success, and how you’ll measure team impact.

- Listening session (35–55 min) — open, structured
  - Prompt 1 — What’s working well? (5 minutes): “What should we definitely keep doing?”
  - Prompt 2 — Biggest bottlenecks today? (10 minutes): “What regularly slows us down or causes rework? Be specific — process, approvals, tech debt, dependencies?”
  - Prompt 3 — Biggest opportunity/idea? (5–10 minutes): “If we had bandwidth to improve one product area in the next quarter, what would it be and why?”

30-60-90 plan — Senior Product Manager
Goal: Transition from operator to strategist + team leader, align product strategy with company goals, and deliver early, measurable impact.

Structure for each period: Objective | Key actions | Owner(s) | Success criteria / metrics

0–30 days — Learn, assess, and deliver quick wins
- Objective: Build context, credibility, and baseline metrics.
- Key actions:
  - Listening tour: 1:1s with manager, direct reports, PM peers, engineering leads, design, sales, CS, marketing, and key customers/partners (schedule ~15–30m each).
  - Read: roadmap, specs, OKRs, analytics dashboards, customer research, incident postmortems, backlog, current sprint.
  - Metrics baseline: ensure product analytics and dashboards (activation, retention, conversion, MAU/DAU, funnel metrics) are accessible and accurate.
  - Process review: observe sprint cadence, grooming, release process, planning, and decision‑making norms.
  - Quick wins: unblock a stalled ticket, improve a recurring meeting, ship a small high-impact bugfix or UX tweak.
  - Communicate: send brief intro to your team; schedule recurring 1:1s and team syncs.
- Owner(s): You + engineering/design leads, manager for context.
- Success criteria:
  - All key stakeholders met; dependencies mapped.
  - Dashboards established and baseline metrics documented.
  - At least one quick win delivered.
  - Shared 30‑60‑90 intent with manager for feedback.

31–60 days — Synthesize, prioritize, and start shaping strategy
- Objective: Turn learnings into prioritized opportunities and align stakeholders on near-term roadmap.
- Key actions:
  - Synthesis: consolidate insights from interviews and data; identify top 3–5 product opportunities and biggest risks.
  - Prioritization: propose prioritization framework (e.g., RICE, ICE) and apply to backlog.
  - Define short-term roadmap: 30–90 day roadmap with clear objectives and metrics for each initiative.
  - Team processes: introduce improvements (e.g., clearer definition of done, better PR review workflow, prioritization ceremonies).
  - Stakeholder alignment: present findings and proposed priorities to manager and cross-functional stakeholders; get buy-in.
  - Start execution: kick off highest-priority initiatives and deliver first scoped features or experiments.
  - People: assess team skill gaps and hiring needs; begin recruiting if required.
- Owner(s): You, product team, engineering/design, PM manager.
- Success criteria:
  - Documented prioritized roadmap with metrics and success definitions.
  - 1–2 initiatives/experiments in flight or shipped with tracked outcomes.
  - Stakeholder alignment and visible process improvements.
  - Hiring plan / resource adjustments identified.

61–90 days — Execute, measure impact, and scale
- Objective: Deliver measurable outcomes, refine strategy, and embed repeatable processes.
- Key actions:
  - Deliver outcomes: complete high-priority features/experiments and measure impact vs. baseline.
  - Roadmap & OKRs: finalize 3–6 month roadmap and link product work to company OKRs.
  - Reporting cadence: publish a regular product report/dashboard and run monthly reviews.
  - Team development: set growth plans, mentor PMs, clarify ownership areas and career paths.
  - Cross-functional partnerships: cement SLAs and communication channels with Sales, CS, Marketing, and Engineering.
  - Optimize: iterate on processes, reduce cycle times, raise quality and predictability.
- Owner(s): You + cross-functional leads.
- Success criteria:
  - Measurable improvements (examples: +X% conversion, reduced lead time by Y%, improved NPS by Z points).
  - Stable, agreed-upon roadmap and reporting cadence.
  - Team clarity on roles, responsibilities, and next steps for development/hiring.
  - Demonstrable stakeholder satisfaction and momentum.

- Time to market: cycle time, lead time, deployment frequency
- Quality: bug rate, production incidents, escape rate
- Customer outcomes: NPS, CSAT, churn, expansion revenue
- Team health: predictability (% of committed scope delivered), sprint velocity trends

- Reduce triage time by introducing a simple bug-priority rubric.
- Run a short usability test and implement a small UX fix with measurable impact.
- Consolidate and share a single source of truth for product metrics.

3) 30/60/90-day plan — focus: Project Orion stabilization + release cadence

Principles: Listen first, triage high-risk items, create repeatable release controls, measure outcomes, then scale.

First 30 days — Stabilize and learn (Listen, triage, and unblock)
Objectives
- Understand current state of Project Orion and release pipeline end-to-end.
- Build trust/rapport with your six direct reports and Alex for handoff.
- Identify critical blockers and deliver 1–2 immediate mitigations.

Actions
- Day 1 align with manager: confirm top 3 priorities and success criteria for Orion and release cadence.
- 1:1s with direct reports (60 min first meeting): priorities, current blockers, dependencies, personal goals.
- 1:1 with Alex (90 min): complete handoff — active issues, stakeholder map, known technical debt, doc locations.
- Cross-functional discovery sessions (30–60 min each): Eng leads, QA, DevOps, Product Marketing, CS, Sales, Legal (if relevant).
- Run a “Release Forensics” session: map the last 3 Orion releases — incidents, root causes, rollback events, customer impact.
- Audit CI/CD pipeline and test coverage with DevOps/QA to find immediate failure points.
- Establish a temporary Orion war-room channel and daily 15-min standup for rapid coordination.

Deliverables / Metrics
- 1–2 implemented quick mitigations (example: temporary freeze on non-critical changes, hotfix for top bug, improved rollback script).
- Listening report (1–2 pages): state, top 5 risks, stakeholders, recommended quick wins.
- Initial baseline metrics collected: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, Mean Time to Recovery (MTTR).

Days 31–60 — Align strategy and implement process changes (Improve cadence)
Objectives
- Define and communicate a stabilized release process for Orion (release readiness checks, gating).
- Start implementing automation and process fixes to reduce manual risk.
- Create visibility via dashboards and stakeholder cadence.

Actions
- Run a release retrospective with key engineers and stakeholders; codify lessons into an actionable plan.
- Introduce a release readiness checklist (code freeze rules, QA signoffs, performance/runbook checks, rollback plan).
- Implement or prioritize automated smoke/regression tests for the highest-risk flows in Orion.
- Create a release calendar and stick to a regular cadence (e.g., weekly or biweekly + emergency hotfix process).
- Establish a metrics dashboard (deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, MTTR, customer incidents) and share weekly.
- Begin delegating ownership for specific release elements to team members (test coverage owner, rollback owner, monitoring owner).

Deliverables / Metrics
- Release readiness checklist adopted for each Orion release.
- Automated smoke tests covering top X user journeys (define X based on app).
- Dashboard published; weekly stakeholder update scheduled.
- Target example (to adapt to your baselines): reduce failed releases by 30% vs. last quarter; cut average hotfix response time by 50%.

Days 61–90 — Execute, measure, and scale (Sustainability)
Objectives
- Deliver the first stable Orion release under the new process.
- Institutionalize release cadence and continuous improvement practices.
- Start longer-term investments (test automation backlog, release pipeline improvements).

Actions
- Lead the release planning and run the stabilized launch for Orion; capture post-release metrics and run a formal postmortem.
- Formalize release roles and runbook; ensure on-call responsibilities and escalation paths are clear.
- Propose a roadmap for medium-term platform work (parallelizable CI improvements, feature flags, canary deployments).
- Start performance reviews/development plans for direct reports focused on release excellence.

Deliverables / Metrics
- Successful Orion release with X% reduction in incidents vs baseline (agree X after baseline).
- Postmortem published with action items tracked and owners assigned.
- Roadmap for CI/CD and automation improvements (quarterly plan).
- Team development plans in place.

Suggested KPIs and examples to track
- Deployment frequency (releases per week/month)
- Lead time for changes (code commit -> production)
- Change failure rate (percent of releases requiring rollback/hotfix)
- MTTR (time to recover from production issue)
- Customer-facing incident count and severity for Orion

Week 1 detailed checklist
- Day 0 (before Monday): Quick note to team/manager: “Looking forward to starting Monday; I’ll schedule 1:1s and a team intro.”
- Day 1: Align with manager (30–60m) to confirm success metrics for Orion and release cadence.
- Days 2–5: 1:1s with each direct report (45–60m) and a 90m with Alex for handoff.
- Organize a 30–45m team intro/all-hands: share your priorities (stabilize Orion, improve cadence), listening posture, immediate next steps.

- Which recurring release issues cause the most pain? (tests, infra, coordination, scope creep)
- What blockers are preventing us from releasing reliably?
- How do you prefer to be supported during high-pressure releases?
- What small change could we make this week to improve confidence in releases?

Quick wins you can pursue in month 1
- Freeze non-essential changes for the next Orion release and communicate scope clearly.
- Create a one-page release checklist and require signoffs from QA and DevOps before cutover.
- Patch or automate the top 1–2 flaky tests to speed up CI feedback.
- Implement a simple canary or feature flag for Orion changes that risk critical flows.
- Remove or shorten one unnecessary recurring meeting that slows decisions.

Templates I can also provide

- A polished slide (1–2 slides) summarizing your 30/60/90 to share at your first all-hands.
- Pre-written status update template for weekly Orion release emails.

Handwritten letter (longer)
Dear [Friend’s name / Nickname],

I still can’t stop thinking about the scrapbook and video you made for my birthday. I kept going back to pages and clips—laughing, crying, and remembering little moments I’d almost forgotten—until I felt wrapped in all the ways you’ve been there for me. You somehow collected the exact pieces of us: the ticket stub from our first concert, the silly note from that midnight diner night, and every tiny inside joke that makes me grin (especially when you call me “[Silly nickname]”).

That gift didn’t just give me memories back—it made me feel seen. You put time, thought, and so much care into something only someone who really knows me could create. I don’t say it enough: you matter to me so deeply. I’m grateful for your quiet loyalty, your terrible jokes that I secretly love, and for all the nights and days that have become “us.” I can’t wait for the next concert, the next late-night diner run, and a hundred more small moments like these.

Thank you for making my birthday unforgettable and for being the person I want beside me through everything. With all my love,  
[Your name]

Low-key “recreate-a-day” plan (introverted, private, modest budget)
Overview: Three gentle stops that echo your shared memories — coffee + small gift, a private “concert” moment, and an intimate midnight-diner-style finish. Keep it low-stimulus, flexible, and cozy.

Timing suggestion
- Start mid-afternoon (so it doesn’t feel rushed). End late evening with the diner vibe (you can aim for a “midnight” feel whenever you both are comfortable).

Stops and what to do
1) Coffee + small keepsake (30–45 minutes)
- Meet at your favorite quiet café or bring coffee to-go and sit on a bench/at home.
- Give them a single Polaroid/photo from the scrapbook (or a printed photo) with a one-line note on the back: “For more naps/coffee/concerts” (or another inside joke).
- Hand them the day’s schedule in a small card: “A few tiny memories, just for you.”

2) Private “first concert” moment (45–60 minutes)
- Recreate the concert feeling at home or a quiet outdoor spot:
  - Make a playlist of the songs you heard at that first concert (or the one or two songs that mean the most).
  - Dim lights / bring string lights, put on the playlist, and play a short clip of you both singing or talking about the first time you went. If you have the original ticket stub, bring it and show it.
  - Keep it short: 1–2 songs and a little chat about how nervous/excited/wild that night was.
- Optional small touch: print the concert photo or ticket and place it in a small frame ($).

3) Midnight diner re-creation (cozy, private)
- If a 24-hour diner is feasible and low-stress, go there; otherwise, recreate it at home:
  - Home setup: dim the lights, play a diner playlist (soft rock/Americana/oldies), make pancakes or order diner-style takeout (milkshake, fries, pie).
  - Set up a small “booth” with cushions, a small candle or battery tealight, and a napkin-wrapped fork. Keep it relaxed.
- During dessert, hand them the handwritten letter. You can either let them read it in private or read aloud the short version below.

Polaroid / photo idea
- Bring 3 instant photos to give at each stop: one at coffee, one at the concert moment, one at the diner. Stick them into a tiny envelope with a one-liner on each back. These then become “future scrapbook” material to add to the one they made.

What to bring (checklist)
- Handwritten letter in an envelope
- 3 printed/Polaroid photos and small envelopes
- Playlist ready on your phone + portable speaker (low volume)
- Small keepsake (framed photo, pressed flower, cheap engraved keychain, or a playlist/USB mix labeled “First Concert — For [Nickname]”)
- Cozy blanket / cushions, battery candles, napkins
- Snacks or diner-style takeout (or ingredients for pancakes/milkshake)

Short script (what to say when you hand the letter)
- If you want a short thing to say: “I wanted to make you a day of small things that felt like the way you made me feel—seen and loved. Thank you for the scrapbook. This is for you.”
- If you want to read a line from the letter aloud: “You put so much care into something only someone who really knows me could create. Thank you for making me feel seen.”

Budget-friendly keepsake ideas
- Frame one favorite photo from their scrapbook ($10–15 frame), or make a small digital playlist card with a printed QR code to a playlist of songs that remind you of them.
- Press a small flower from a walk and tuck it into the envelope with your letter.
- Polaroids are inexpensive in small numbers, or print phone photos at a local drugstore.

Want me to finalize?
- I can personalize the letter with the friend’s real name and the actual silly nickname if you’d like.
- I can draft a short text to send them asking for the date/time (if you’re inviting them) or a subtle invite line if you want it to feel spontaneous but gentle.

Would you like me to insert names now, or tweak the tone (more playful, more formal, funnier, etc.)?

messages.speaker: responder_agent
messages.content:
This is lovely — the scrapbook shows they pay attention to the small, emotional things. Here are a variety of thoughtful-return ideas you can pick from or mix and match, with quick, practical ways to make each one feel just as meaningful.

- Mini handmade scrapbook or “reasons I love you” book
  - Make a small book with photos, tickets, and 30–50 short handwritten notes (one per page) — each note a memory, trait you adore, or a tiny future promise.
  - Personalize fonts/ink colors, add little drawings or stickers. Tie it with ribbon.

- Memory jar or “open when” letters
  - Fill a jar with folded notes: memories, prompts (“open when you feel…”) or coupons.
  - For “open when” letters, write 6–12 envelopes (e.g., open when you’re tired, when you need a laugh, when you miss me).

- Surprise experience day tailored to them
  - Plan a day around their favorites (breakfast at a favorite café, visit a meaningful spot, a class/workshop they’d love).
  - Include small surprises during the day (a playlist for the drive, a handwritten itinerary, a picnic with foods they love).

- Scavenger hunt that leads to a personal gift
  - Create 4–6 clues referencing shared memories or inside jokes, each clue leading to a small item or note, final destination reveals a gift or a reunion.
  - Use photos or location-based clues for extra nostalgia.

- Photo/video montage or short film
  - Compile photos and short clips set to music with voiceover narration telling your story together.
  - End with a personal message or a “ticket” to a planned date.

- Create a themed “date night in” kit
  - Choose a theme they love (favorite movie, country cuisine, museum night). Include printed invitations, menu, playlist, props, and a handwritten note explaining why you chose it.

- Plant or time-capsule with a promise
  - Gift a plant with a note about growing together, or bury a small time capsule you both fill with notes/maps/photos to open on a future anniversary.

- DIY keepsake (framed photo collage, engraved item, custom map)
  - Frame a photo collage with annotations, or get a small engraved keychain/pendant with coordinates/date — something they can carry.

- A personalized playlist + explanation booklet
  - Curate a playlist of songs that map to phases of your relationship and include a little booklet explaining why each song made the cut.

- Host a “micro-ceremony”
  - Create a short intimate ceremony at home or a favorite spot where you exchange handwritten vows/letters and share a favorite meal — keep it low-pressure, heartfelt, and short.

Quick tips to match the scrapbook magic
- Handwritten beats printed: keep handwriting, doodles, and small imperfections.
- Small, specific details matter: reference a particular day, phrase, or memory that only you two share.
- Sensory touches: add a spritz of a familiar cologne, include a pressed flower, or use scrapbook paper that evokes a memory.
- Presentation: wrap simply but thoughtfully (brown paper + twine + a sprig) or include a small reveal moment.

If you want, I can:
- Draft 10–20 “reasons I love you” notes or “open when” letters.
- Help write scavenger-hunt clues tailored to your shared memories.
- Outline a full experience-day schedule with timing and logisitics.
Tell me a bit about your partner’s interests, any budget/time constraints, and whether you want something surprise-y or collaborative — I’ll tailor a plan.

messages.speaker: responder_agent
messages.content:
This is such a sweet brief — I love the vibe. Below are (A) ~20 short, handwritten-style “reasons I love you” notes you can write into little cards, and (B) a 5-stop, mostly-surprise scavenger-hunt plan tailored to cozy vinyl/coffee nights, nostalgic surprises, and hikes, ending with two final-options (vinyl or picnic). I’ve included exact clue texts you can copy, what to hide at each stop, setup tips, budget notes, and a quick timeline for doing it all in a week. If you want, I can personalize the clues to real places/inside jokes once you tell me a couple of specific spots or names.

A. ~20 “Reasons I love you” notes (short, one-line; write each on a little card)
1. You make the smallest moments feel like something sacred.  
2. You hum the songs I didn’t know I loved.  
3. Your coffee-making routine smells like home.  
4. You remember tiny details no one else notices.  
5. You hold my hand like you mean it — always.  
6. You laugh at my dumb jokes and make them better.  
7. You know when I need quiet and when I need company.  
8. You make hikes feel like adventures, not chores.  
9. You dance while you’re cooking and it becomes the best part of dinner.  
10. You keep old things (and people) with such reverence.  
11. You ask questions that make me think and feel.  
12. You make vinyl crackles sound like the soundtrack of us.  
13. You make rainy Sundays into the coziest days ever.  
14. You’ve taught me patience, and you’ve taught me playfulness.  
15. You believe in my ideas when I can’t quite yet.  
16. You remember my order without looking it up.  
17. You make nostalgia feel sweet, not sad.  
18. You always share the last bite.  
19. You build small rituals with me — they mean everything.  
20. You love me in ways I didn’t know I needed.

B. Scavenger-hunt plan (5 stops) — final reveal: choose either a vinyl gift or a picnic
Overview: 5 clues, mostly hidden in/around your home + one outdoor stop (short walk/hike). Each stop has a tiny token and a clue leading to the next. One collaborative moment: at clue 3 they pick a song to add to a joint playlist (or record a 10–20s voice memo), which becomes part of the gift.

Materials you’ll need
- 5 small envelopes or folded cards, handwritten (one for each clue)  
- Small tokens for each stop: coffee sachet/gift card, pressed flower/photo, trail-mix bag, Polaroid/printed photo, small wrapped vinyl OR picnic supplies (see below)  
- A blanket, thermos, portable speaker/record player (if you plan vinyl at picnic), utensils/napkins (if picnic)  
- Ribbon/twine and a simple wrap for the final gift  
- Optional: QR code printed linking to a playlist you start (include the song they pick)  
- $50–100 budget breakdown: vinyl $20–40; picnic food/supplies $20–40; small tokens and stationery $10–20

Clue 1 (Start: morning/doorstep)
How to deliver: Put the first envelope on their coffee mug, on the front door, or slide it under their pillow for a morning reveal.  
Clue text to write in the envelope:
"Where our mornings officially begin — follow the scent that wakes us up together."  
What to hide there: a fresh coffee sachet or $5 coffee-shop gift card + the next clue.

Clue 2 (Coffee spot → record player or vinyl shelf)
Where to hide: inside or next to your favorite mug, or taped to your record player.  
Clue text:
"The voice that starts the song and the crackle before the chorus — find the place the needle always finds."  
What to hide there: a small printed “track list” (a few songs that made you think of them) or a tiny paper “ticket” promising a vinyl pick later + next clue.

Clue 3 (Nostalgia/photo spot → scrapbook/album frame)
Where: near the scrapbook/photo wall where you keep sentimental things.  
Clue text:
"Photos, ticket stubs, and that awkward Polaroid — look where we keep small memories that grow big."  
What to hide there: a Polaroid or printed photo of you two, a pressed flower, and the next clue. Also include a small request: "Pick one song right now for our 'Us' playlist — record it on the little card or tell me when I call you in 10 minutes." (This is the small collaborative moment.)  
Why: they get to add a song/voice memo — interactive and sweet.

Clue 4 (Hike/gear spot)
Where to hide: by hiking boots, backpack, or in a pocket of their jacket. If you’ll take them on a short walk, this clue can send them to the trailhead.  
Clue text:
"For days when we chase ridgelines and coffee tastes better at the top — where we lace up to go find a view."  
What to hide there: small bag of trail mix or snack + next clue that’s a small riddle pointing to the final spot (record shop or picnic location).

Clue 5 (Final clue → final reveal location)
Option A — Final reveal is a vinyl:  
- If you can coordinate with a friendly local record shop, arrange to hide the wrapped vinyl there (many indie shops will hold an item if you explain) and make the final clue direct them there. If not, hide the wrapped vinyl at home in a pre-arranged place (e.g., under the couch cushion, in a shoebox at the entry).  
Final clue text (for vinyl):
"Follow the road that leads to the spin — a new record awaits, picked just for you. Go to [record shop name] / the place where music waits."  
What to put as the final gift: a wrapped vinyl (choose an album they already love, or an album you want to introduce them to). Include: a handwritten note saying why you chose that record, plus one of the “reasons I love you” notes tucked inside.

Option B — Final reveal is a picnic with vinyl/coffee:
- Set up at a favorite scenic bench/park/hill — a short hike from clue 4 or at a spot you both love. Bring blanket, thermos of their coffee, pastry/favorite snacks, portable speaker or battery-powered record player if you have one.  
Final clue text (for picnic):
"Turn the next corner and unfold our afternoon — warm coffee, a blanket, and an extra song for the road."  
What to put as the final gift: picnic set-up + the wrapped record (or a small record-themed note) and a stack of several "reasons I love you" cards fanned out. Play the playlist you built (including the song they chose).

Sample riddle-style clues (copy/paste-friendly)
1. "Where mornings come to life — find the mug that knows our names."  
2. "Where vinyl breathes and our room gets warm — look where the needle rests."  
3. "Where snapshots sleep and memories stack — find the frame with that funny hat."  
4. "Where boots meet dirt and views are earned — check the laces that always leave for the weekend."  
5a. (vinyl) "Find your next favorite song where the records are shelved and stories spin."  
5b. (picnic) "Follow the path toward the bench that watches the sunset — unfold our afternoon."

Presentation & small touches
- Handwrite everything; use different ink colors or a smear of your cologne on the very last note for a sensory cue.  
- Press a small flower from a past hike into one envelope.  
- Add a tiny printed QR code linking to the playlist you started (include the song they added).  
- Keep the tokens meaningful, small, and inexpensive: coffee sachet, Polaroid, trail-mix bag, small candle, or a used concert ticket in a frame.  
- If leaving clues in public, either: (a) place them in obvious, safe spots you control (coat, bag, inside a favorite café with owner permission), or (b) keep all hiding at home and end with a picnic or record-shop reveal to avoid logistics.

Quick timeline (one week)
Day 1: Buy vinyl or confirm record shop hold; buy small tokens and stationery.  
Day 2: Handwrite clues and notes; create playlist and print QR code.  
Day 3: Assemble little tokens into envelopes; press any flowers/print photos.  
Day 4: Practice the route (if outdoors) and confirm final spot availability.  
Day 5: Finalize wrapping and any store coordination.  
Day 6: Set up the night before for indoor clues; for outdoor/hike, set most up the day of unless you’re hiding in a public place (then hide only what’s safe to leave).  
Day 7: The reveal day — deliver clue #1 in the morning or before your planned time.

Budget suggestions
- Vinyl: $20–40 (used records are often cheaper and can be extra-nostalgic)  
- Picnic food & coffee supplies: $10–30 depending on snacks (homemade is budget-friendly)  
- Tokens/stationery: $10–20  
- Portable speaker/record player: borrow one if you don’t already own it to keep under budget

Want me to:
- Personalize the 5 clues with actual places/phrases/inside jokes? (I can rewrite them so they’re perfectly specific.)  
- Draft exact wording for each physical card and the final note inside the vinyl/picnic wrap?  
- Pick vinyl suggestions based on their taste (name a few artists they like)?

Which final option do you prefer — vinyl or picnic — and do you want the clues customized to any specific spots or nicknames?

Make sure one clue asks them to add a song to the playlist and tuck several “reasons I love you” cards into the final picnic wrap — I’m so excited!

Timing suggestion

Tell me which of those (or both) and I’ll write them out exactly so you can copy/paste or handwrite.

Ideas (grouped by vibe)

- Micro‑gesture day (mirror what they did)
  - Plan a full day of tiny, meaningful moments: favorite breakfast, a handwritten note at each stop, a short playlist cued for different times, a quick massage, a favorite dessert at sunset. Ten little surprises can feel as big as one grand gesture.

- Scavenger hunt that builds to a memory
  - Send them on a route of meaningful locations (where you met, first date, favorite café), each stop with a small gift or a note. Final stop: a picnic, private dinner, or a surprise experience you arranged.

- Keepsake creations
  - Make them a “year two” scrapbook or a jar of 365 notes (one for each day). Commission a custom illustration/painting of a favorite photo or the place you met. Frame a star‑map print of the night you first met.

- Shared adventure experience
  - Book a class you can do together (cooking, pottery, dance), a hot‑air balloon or sunset sail, a weekend cabin getaway, or a curated tasting at home (cheese/wine, chocolate).

- Story & media
  - Produce a short video with clips/messages from friends and family intercut with your favorite photos + their favorite song. Or write and perform (or have someone perform) a short song or poem for them.

- Ritual + promise
  - Plan a private ceremony: exchange new, lighthearted vows or “promises” and bury a time capsule to open in 5 years. Plant a tree together and hang a small plaque.

- Low‑cost deeply personal
  - Cook a multi‑course dinner of dishes from meaningful moments (first meal together, travels, etc.), decorate with photos and the song from your anniversary, end with a handwritten letter.

Execution tips
- Personalize to their love language (words, acts, time, gifts, touch). If they love acts of service, do chores or an organized home surprise; if they love words, lean into letters and videos.
- Build emotional arcs: start small, create suspense (clues or small reveals), and finish with an emotional payoff (a meaningful keepsake or shared experience).
- Keep timing realistic—book restaurants/experiences early. Recruit one or two helpful friends if you need decoys or help placing items.
- Sensory details matter: use their favorite scent, music, or a familiar food to trigger memory.
- Secrecy tips: create plausible distractions (work errands, an outing with a friend), stash items with a friend, send digital clues from a new address/phone if you want to hide the organizer identity.

Quick example: A 5‑stop scavenger hunt
1) “Where we first locked eyes” — small photo from the day + clue
2) Favorite coffee shop — barista hands them a note with the next clue
3) Park bench where you talked all night — a potted plant with a message
4) Bookstore/record store — a copy of a short poem or the song’s lyrics
5) Final spot (picnic at a beach/rooftop/home) — scrapbook you made, candles, playlist cued to their song, and you waiting

Tell me: your partner’s top 3 interests, their love language if you know it, expected budget, and how soon you want to do this. I can draft a step‑by‑step itinerary, provide clue text, shopping lists, and a playlist or script.

- Keep a high-resolution scan (or good photo) saved in multiple places (cloud + external drive) so you have a backup and can print replicas.

Panna Cotta (vanilla) — yields 4 small servings (halve for 2)
Ingredients
- 480 ml (2 cups) heavy cream
- 120 ml (1/2 cup) whole milk
- 50 g (1/4 cup) granulated sugar
- 1 vanilla bean split and scraped (or 1 tsp vanilla extract)
- 7 g (about 2 1/4 tsp / 1 packet) powdered gelatin
- 45 ml (3 tbsp) cold water (for blooming gelatin)

Method & timing
1. Bloom gelatin: sprinkle gelatin over 3 tbsp cold water in a small bowl; let sit 5 minutes.
2. Heat cream mixture: in a saucepan, combine cream, milk, sugar and the vanilla bean seeds + pod (or extract). Warm over medium heat until just starting to steam and sugar dissolves — do not boil (about 4–6 minutes).
3. Add gelatin: remove pan from heat, discard the vanilla pod (if used), stir in bloomed gelatin until fully dissolved (1 minute).
4. Strain (optional): for extra silkiness, pour through a fine mesh into a measuring jug.
5. Pour into ramekins or small glasses. Let cool at room temp 15–20 minutes, then cover and refrigerate until set, minimum 4 hours (overnight is best).
Total active time: ~15–20 minutes. Chill: 4+ hours.

Unmolding (if desired)
- Run a thin-bladed knife around the edge, dip ramekin bottoms in hot water 5–7 seconds (don’t submerge), invert onto plate and lift. If serving in glasses, just serve chilled.

Berry Compote (quick topping)
Ingredients
- 200 g (1 cup) mixed berries (fresh or frozen)
- 2 tbsp sugar (adjust to taste)
- 1 tsp lemon juice
- 1 tbsp water (if berries are dry)

Method & timing
1. In a small saucepan, combine berries, sugar, lemon juice and 1 tbsp water.
2. Cook over medium-low heat, stirring occasionally, until berries break down and sauce is slightly thickened, 5–7 minutes.
3. Cool to room temp, then chill. Spoon over panna cotta just before serving.
Optional: stir in a few drops of balsamic vinegar for a savory-sweet lift or garnish with grated lemon zest and a mint leaf.

Make-ahead notes
- You can make panna cotta up to 48 hours ahead. Compote keeps 3–4 days refrigerated.
- For a lighter panna cotta, swap 60–80 ml of cream for more milk; for richer, use all cream.

Other

Notes: buy prepackaged or clearly labeled peanut‑free items only and avoid shared bulk bins. If you order any prepared items from a shop, explicitly state “vegetarian, peanut allergy — no peanuts or peanut oil, no cross‑contact.”

Timed cooking & setup plan (day‑of, for a 7:30 PM dinner)
Overview & assumptions
- You’ll place the cards/mementos around town earlier in the day (separate from cooking).
- You’ll prepare/cook in your kitchen and transport or hold dishes on the rooftop in insulated containers or in a low oven (if rooftop has no stove).
- Aim to be fully finished with major cooking and rooftop setup so you can wait at the rooftop for Sam. The hunt starts at 5:30 PM as planned and Sam arrives at rooftop ~7:30 PM.

Suggested schedule (day‑of; start early to stay relaxed)
Morning / day before
- Day before (or morning): grocery shop. Pre‑chop any veg you can (dice tomatoes for bruschetta, chop onion/shallot, clean mushrooms if you use them), make any dressings/vinaigrettes, and chill dessert (or buy sorbet). Store everything labeled.

3:00 PM — Rooftop setup (if you’ll be there placing lights early)
- String lights, set table for 2, arrange battery candles, set speaker & playlist, place small potted herb/floral sprig.
- Lay out plates/napkins, set aside serving bowls and utensils. Put insulated containers or warming dish in place.

3:45 PM — Start cooking
- Preheat oven to 400–425°F (200–220°C).
- Prepare stuffed pepper filling:
  - Cook 1/2 cup long‑grain rice according to package (yield ~1¼ cups cooked). Or use leftover cooked rice from day before.
  - In a skillet: 1 tbsp olive oil, sauté 1/2 finely chopped onion/shallot until soft. Add 1 clove minced garlic for 1 minute. Add 1/2 cup corn kernels, rinsed black beans (≈3/4 cup drained), 1/2 cup diced tomatoes (or 2 tbsp tomato paste + splash water), cumin 1/2 tsp, smoked paprika 1/4–1/2 tsp, salt/pepper. Stir for 2–3 min.
  - Stir in cooked rice, 2 tbsp chopped cilantro/parsley, adjust seasoning. Spoon into halved bell peppers, top with shredded cheese (about 1/2 cup total). Place in a small baking dish with a little water in bottom.
- Put stuffed peppers in oven: bake ~30–35 min until peppers are tender and cheese melted.
- While peppers bake: prepare potatoes.

4:20 PM — Garlic‑roasted baby potatoes
- Toss baby potatoes (400 g) with 1–2 tbsp olive oil, 3 minced garlic cloves, salt, pepper, and a little thyme or rosemary. Roast at 400–425°F for 35–40 min, turning halfway, until golden and crisp. Remove and keep warm in a low oven (200°F) or in an insulated container.

4:45 PM — Charred asparagus & bruschetta prep
- Asparagus: toss with a little olive oil, salt, pepper. Roast 8–12 min at 425°F or pan‑sear on high heat 6–8 min (tender‑crisp). Keep warm.
- Bruschetta topping: dice 3 tomatoes, mix with minced garlic (1 clove), chopped basil, 1 tbsp olive oil, 1 tsp balsamic, salt/pepper. Let sit covered in fridge. Slice baguette and lightly toast/broil 4–6 min until crisp; wrap and keep at room temp.

5:20–5:40 PM — Final checks & hold food warm
- Remove all dishes; keep them warm in oven at 200°F or transfer into insulated carriers. Cover tins with foil.
- Put final mementos/cards in place if any last minute.
- Quick taste check and adjust seasoning.
- Put bruschetta topping in a sealed container in the fridge (assemble on site).

5:30 PM — Cards/hunt start
- You should have placed cards earlier, or placed them now if someone can watch the rooftop. You will be waiting at the rooftop for Sam’s arrival.

6:45–7:10 PM — Final rooftop finishing (if you’re there)
- If food is on site and needs a quick reheat: pop stuffed peppers in oven 5–8 minutes at 425°F to reheat and refresh the cheese, or spoon into a serving dish and warm under a lamp or in warming container. Reheat potatoes for 5–10 min if needed.
- Assemble bruschetta at the last minute: spoon topping onto toasted baguette slices just before serving to keep bread crisp.
- Reheat asparagus if needed (quick pan or oven for 3–4 min).
- Plate or bring food to table in serving dishes, set wine/mocktail station, light candles.

7:30 PM — Sam arrives; serve
- Place final handwritten letter on the table for Sam to read after a toast.
- Keep conversation easy; finish with the sorbet and berries.

Quick make‑ahead suggestions & reheating tips
- Stuffed peppers: excellent to make earlier and reheat; they hold shape and flavor.
- Potatoes: reheat in a hot oven (400°F) for 6–10 min to regain crispness; if not possible, heat in a skillet with a little oil.
- Asparagus: quick pan‑sear on site for 2–3 min if you want fresh char.
- Bruschetta: keep topping chilled and bread toasted separately to avoid sogginess.
- If you used any prepared sauces or store items, verify peanut‑free labeling.

Exact lasagna recipe (9x13 pan — serves 4; prep times included)
Notes: If you use oven-ready noodles, no pre-boil. If you assemble and refrigerate, add 10–15 minutes to the bake time when baking from cold.

Ingredients
- 1 lb ground beef (or 1/2 lb beef + 1/2 lb Italian sausage)
- 1 small onion, finely chopped
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 2 (24 oz) jars marinara sauce (about 48 oz total) OR 28 oz crushed tomatoes + 6 oz tomato paste + 1 cup water
- 12 lasagna noodles (regular or oven-ready)
- 15 oz ricotta cheese
- 1 large egg
- 2 tbsp chopped fresh parsley (or 1 tsp dried)
- 2 cups shredded mozzarella (about 8 oz) + 1 cup extra for topping
- 1 cup grated Parmesan
- 2 tbsp olive oil
- Salt, pepper, 1 tsp Italian seasoning, pinch red pepper flakes (optional)

Steps & timing
Total active prep ≈ 45–60 min (plus simmer time). If assembling earlier, refrigerate until bake.

1) Sauce (start ~2:45–3:15 PM if you’re prepping ahead)
- Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a medium pot over medium heat. Add chopped onion, cook 5–7 minutes until translucent. Add garlic, cook 30–60 sec.
- Add ground beef (and sausage if using). Brown, breaking up, 6–8 minutes. Drain excess fat if needed.
- Stir in marinara sauce (or crushed tomatoes + tomato paste + 1 cup water). Add 1 tsp Italian seasoning, salt & pepper to taste, pinch of red pepper flakes. Simmer 15–20 minutes, stirring occasionally. Turn off and set aside to cool slightly.

2) Ricotta mixture (10 minutes)
- In a bowl, combine 15 oz ricotta, 1 egg, 2 tbsp chopped parsley, 1/2 cup grated Parmesan (reserve some for topping), salt and pepper to taste. Mix gently.

3) Noodles
- If using regular noodles: boil per package instructions until al dente (usually 8–10 min). Drain and lay on a lightly oiled sheet to prevent sticking. If oven-ready, skip this.

4) Assemble (30 minutes)
- Preheat oven to 350°F when you’re about 45–60 minutes from dinner if baking right away; otherwise assemble and refrigerate.
- Spread ~1 cup sauce on the bottom of a greased 9x13 pan.
- Layer: 3–4 noodles (depending on noodle size), 1/3 ricotta mixture (spread), 1/3 sauce, 1/3 mozzarella. Repeat two more times so you end with sauce and cheese on top. Sprinkle remaining 1 cup mozzarella and remaining Parmesan on top.
- Cover tightly with foil (spray foil with nonstick spray or make sure cheese doesn't stick).

5) Bake (timed for dinner at ~7:30 PM)
- If assembled and refrigerated: remove from fridge 20–30 minutes before baking to warm slightly. Bake covered at 350°F for 45–55 minutes (because it's cold), then uncover and bake 8–10 minutes more to brown the top.
- If assembled fresh at room temp: bake covered at 350°F for 35–40 minutes, uncover and bake 8–10 minutes until cheese is golden.
- Let rest 8–12 minutes before cutting so it sets.

Timed lava cake recipe (2 ramekins; 350°F)
Ingredients (2 servings)
- 4 oz bittersweet chocolate, chopped
- 4 tbsp (1/4 cup / 56 g) unsalted butter
- 2 whole eggs + 2 egg yolks (or 3 whole eggs if you prefer)
- 1/4 cup (50 g) granulated sugar
- 2 tbsp (16 g) all-purpose flour
- 1/2 tsp vanilla extract
- Pinch of salt
- Butter + cocoa powder or flour for ramekins
- Ice cream/whipped cream and berries to serve

Steps & timing
Total active prep ≈ 15–20 min (plus chill if you refrigerate)

1) Prep ramekins (5 min)
- Butter two 6–8 oz ramekins and dust with cocoa powder (or flour). Place on a baking sheet.

2) Make batter (10 min)
- Melt chocolate and butter together gently in a double boiler or microwave in 20–30 sec bursts, stirring until smooth. Let cool 1–2 minutes.
- Whisk eggs, egg yolks, and sugar until pale and slightly thickened (about 1–2 minutes). Stir in vanilla.
- Fold melted chocolate into the egg mixture, then gently fold in flour and a pinch of salt until just combined.

3) Chill (optional 30 min–several hours)
- For a more reliable center, pour batter into ramekins, cover, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes (you can do this earlier in afternoon). Chilling helps the exterior set while the center stays molten when baked.

4) Bake (timed during dessert service)
- Preheat oven to 350°F (if not already warm).
- If batter was refrigerated, bake at 350°F for 12–14 minutes. If batter at room temp, bake 10–12 minutes. Edges should be set and puffed; centers slightly jiggly.
- Let sit 1 minute, then carefully invert onto plates: run a knife around edge, place plate over ramekin and flip. Serve immediately with ice cream and berries.

- 2:00–3:00 PM: Grocery run / buy extras.
- 3:00 PM: Start sauce (prep + simmer ~30 min).
- 3:45–4:15 PM: Boil noodles (if using regular), make ricotta mix, shred cheese if needed.

- 5:15–6:30 PM: Set table, candles, playlist; prep salad and starter so they’re ready to finish later.
- 6:45 PM: Preheat oven to 350°F.

- 7:30 PM: Remove lasagna, rest 8–12 min while you finish salad and warm plates; greet Alex and serve.
- ~8:15–8:20 PM (after a relaxed main + a little conversation): Bake lava cakes 10–14 min at 350°F; serve warm with ice cream.

Final small touches & tips
- Warm plates for 30–60 seconds in the warm oven before serving (use caution).
- Put the handwritten note on Alex’s plate or slip it into an envelope and hand it to them after they sit.
- If you’re nervous about inverting the lava cakes, serve them in the ramekins with a spoon — still very cozy and low-pressure.

Concept: A scavenger-style “memory trail” through meaningful places that ends at a surprise dinner where friends present a new collaborative scrapbook/video montage and a special experience gift for your friend.

High-level plan
- Timeline: 2–3 weeks prep.
- Guests: 6–12 close friends (or scale down to just 1–3 if you prefer intimate).
- Budget: flexible — basic $100–$300 (crafts + food) ; mid $300–$800 (venue, printed photos, small gifts); higher if you rent a space or book an experience.
- Big moment: Friends re-create 3–4 favorite memories at stations (or photos reenacted), capture new photos/polaroids, then gather for a surprise dinner with a slideshow and a new scrapbook page that everyone contributed to.

Step-by-step
1. Pick 3–4 meaningful locations (café where you met, park bench, concert venue, their favorite bakery). Short walking distance or a quick drive between spots.
2. Plan small activities at each stop that match the scrapbook pages:
   - Stop 1 (Meet-cute spot): Give them a quick clue; re-create the first photo with a Polaroid and hand them a small printed note from an old text/conversation.
   - Stop 2 (Inside joke spot): Play a 1–2 minute audio clip from you or a friend telling the memory, then take a goofy group photo.
   - Stop 3 (Favorite snack place): Arrange to have their favorite treat waiting and a friend there for a hug and a new message to add to the scrapbook.
3. Clues/scavenger hunt: Create 4-6 simple, nostalgic clues that lead them from place to place. (Examples below.)
4. Finale: The last clue leads them to the dinner location (private dining room, reserved table, decorated backyard). Friends are hidden and then appear when they arrive. Have a slideshow/video montage playing and the new collaborative scrapbook waiting.
5. Gift: Present a framed “future memories” page — include a ticket to an experience you know they want (concert, weekend trip, workshop) tucked into an envelope glued to the page.
6. Document: Ask everyone to add a handwritten note or a Polaroid to the scrapbook during dinner.

Materials & logistics
- Materials: Polaroid or instant-print camera, printed photos, scrapbook page supplies, envelopes for clues, small props for reenactments, playlist, projector or laptop for slideshow.
- Coordination: Create a group chat for friends to confirm availability, photo/video contributions, and small tasks (decorate, bring food, man a station).
- Permissions & pacing: Check the friend’s availability and any mobility/comfort constraints; pick easy travel between stops.

Simple lavender‑honey shortbread recipe (yields ~18–24 small cookies)
Ingredients
- 2 cups (250 g) all‑purpose flour
- 1 cup (227 g) unsalted butter, room temperature
- 1/2 cup (60 g) powdered sugar (or granulated sugar if preferred)
- 2 tbsp honey
- 1–2 tsp dried culinary lavender, lightly crushed
- 1 tsp vanilla extract
- Pinch of salt
Optional finish: a light honey drizzle or a dusting of powdered sugar

Steps
1. Preheat oven to 325°F (165°C). Line a baking sheet with parchment.
2. Cream the butter and sugar until smooth. Beat in honey and vanilla.
3. Mix in the crushed lavender and salt.
4. Gradually add the flour until a soft dough forms. Don’t overwork.
5. Shape into a log, or press into a small square pan and chill 20–30 minutes until firm.
6. Slice (if log) into 1/4–1/2‑inch rounds or cut shapes from pressed dough. Place on baking sheet.
7. Bake 18–22 minutes until edges are lightly golden. Cool completely on a rack.
8. Optional: drizzle a little honey or dust powdered sugar before serving. Store in an airtight tin.

Timing & extras
- Total active time: ~30 min; chill/bake time: ~40–50 min.
- Print the recipe on a card and sign it “From our kitchen — a little piece of Grandma.”
- Present the finished cookies in a decorated tin with one of the notes above attached.

Surprise plan B — Keepsake jar and recipe card
Why it works: a physical reminder connecting the remembered detail to ongoing thoughtfulness.

- Attach a tag that reads: “Because you remembered the lavender‑honey shortbread — thank you for seeing me.”

Presentation ideas

- Combine with one or two homemade cookies and the medium note; they’ll get the emotional connection and a sweet treat.

Combine both (my recommendation)
- Bake together and, when the cookies are done, present one decorated tin or keepsake jar with the recipe card and a note. That ties the experience and the keepsake, and shows both attention and effort.
